newsitem.title: SPAIN: Air cargo rates ex-Madrid steady, 1997 rise likely.
newsitem.headline: Air cargo rates ex-Madrid steady, 1997 rise likely.

text.p: Cargo rates ex-Madrid are holding steady, excluding a fuel surcharge now being levied by almost all major airlines, but the industry widely expects prices to rise in January, a Reuter survey showed.
The peak season is now well under way and demand for space is particularly strong on Latin American routes, mixed on Far Eastern routes and fair in the highly competitive North American market.

Almost all the airlines and freight forwarders surveyed said their basic rates were unchanged and variations in the average rates given are due to variations in airlines and general sales agents questioned.

"Brazil and Argentina are very strong at the moment and space is selling easily," said the commercial manager at one Latin American airline. "We're taking all kinds of cargo, plenty of components for example."
Iberia said its return trade from Chile was strong as it was peak season for fish and other fresh food exports, but a third airline reported problems filling its west-east South American flights.
Varig said it was struggling to cope with cargo demand to Brazil and that prices were tending to creep up although its own rates had not changed.

Average rates are little different this month - except for the Middle East where the range of prices quoted swings from 195 to 305 pesetas a kilo and the average emerged higher - but several people said they expected rises early next year.
"There will be rises in January for sure," said a freight forwarder. "Rates have tended to go down for the last two years and we've hit the bottom now."
A general sales agent agreed, saying he was expecting a price increase of around three percent by most airlines in January.

Iberia joined other European flag carriers in imposing a 13 peseta (10 US cent) per kilo fuel surcharge, which in theory came into force on November 5, although industry sources said in practice it was taking somewhat longer to apply.
Most people expect the surcharge to be temporary, although some fear it will be replaced immediately by a rise in actual rates.
Airlines have been saying for months that North Atlantic prices have to rise, but competition is as fierce as ever and capacity is still increasing.

"The North Atlantic is still very cheap and very competitive," said a GSA who quoted a price of 180 pesetas a kilo for cargoes of more than 100 kilos to New York but said it was possible to achieve a price of 140 pesetas in some cases.
"We're increasing export shipments to Boston and Dallas particularly and also to New York, much of it spare parts," said a freight forwarder.
Generally the peak export months were going well, airlines said, although there were isolated complaints.

Air France said it thought activity in general, although well above summer levels, was slacker than the same period last year and Iberia said business to Japan had been weak, with a tendency towards lower rates on the return trip, although it looked as if volumes were now recovering.
Demand for space from both Madrid and Barcelona is generally expected to remain high throughout November and December before beginning to slacken early next year.
